**Instructions.** Complete this assignment in Quarto or R Markdown and upload
both your `.qmd` source and the rendered `.html` to Brightspace. Show your code. Interpretation questions are
graded on precision (adjusted for what, units, association vs causation,
population), exactly as practiced in the labs. End with your AI-use statement
(see Section 4).

**Data.** Infant mortality for 105 countries, circa the 1970s. This is a
classic messy dataset: a few countries have missing mortality values, and the
country names stored in the row names carry trailing spaces.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
data(infmort, package = "faraway")
inf <- infmort |>
  na.omit() |>
  rownames_to_column("country") |>
  mutate(country = str_trim(country))
```

Variables used below: `mortality` = infant deaths per 1,000 live births,
`income` = per-capita annual income (US dollars), `region` = Africa, Europe,
Asia, or Americas (Africa is the reference level), `oil` = oil exports or no
oil exports. After dropping missing values, 101 countries remain.

# Section 1: Do (6 points)

**1.1** Show the distributions of `mortality` and `income` with histograms
and a numerical summary of each. One sentence per variable on shape,
mentioning where the mean sits relative to the median. (2 pts)

**1.2** Fit the raw-scale model `mortality ~ income` and the log-log model
`log(mortality) ~ log(income)`. Report both coefficient tables and both
R-squared values, and show the scatterplot on each scale with the fitted line
added. One sentence on which scale the linear model describes better. (2 pts)

**1.3** Extend the log-log model with the categorical predictors:
`log(mortality) ~ log(income) + region + oil`. Report the coefficient table.
(2 pts)

# Section 2: Interpret (8 points; interpretation precision counts double)

**2.1** Interpret the `log(income)` coefficient from the model in 1.3 as an
elasticity, in one strong-form sentence: what percent difference in mortality
is associated with a 1% difference in income, adjusted for what, in what
population? (2 pts)

**2.2** Interpret the `regionEurope` coefficient from 1.3 in one strong-form
sentence, making the reference level explicit. Then convert it to a
multiplicative statement about mortality using `exp()`. (2 pts)

**2.3** Test whether `region` as a whole belongs in the model: compare
`log(mortality) ~ log(income) + oil` to the full model from 1.3 with
`anova()`. State the null hypothesis in words (how many coefficients does it
constrain?), report F and the p-value, and conclude in one sentence. (2 pts)

**2.4** Compute Cook's distances for the model in 1.3 and identify the two
most influential countries (they are both oil exporters). Refit the model
without them and report what happens to the `oil` coefficient and its
p-value, and to the `log(income)` coefficient. Two sentences on what this
tells you about how fragile the oil "effect" is. (2 pts)

# Section 3: Critique the AI (6 points)

A student gave this dataset to an AI assistant and asked for a write-up of
the model from 1.3. The assistant replied:

> "Using the 101 countries with complete data, I fit log mortality on log
> income, region, and oil exports. The income coefficient of -0.34 means that
> each additional dollar of per-capita income lowers infant mortality by 0.34
> deaths per 1,000 live births. Africa does not appear in the coefficient
> table, which tells us the model found no region effect for African
> countries. The coefficient for no oil exports was -0.64; since it is
> negative, we conclude that exporting oil protects a country's infants. The
> joint F test for region gave F = 3.2 with p = 0.03, so the region variable
> is only marginally useful and could reasonably be dropped. Finally, to
> report results on the original scale, I exponentiated the model's predicted
> mean of log mortality, which gives an unbiased estimate of a country's mean
> mortality rate."

**3.1** This paragraph contains at least four distinct statistical errors.
Identify each one you find (quote the offending phrase), and explain in one
or two sentences why it is wrong. Finding four earns full credit; a fifth
earns a bonus point. (4 pts + 1 bonus)

**3.2** Verify the AI's claim about the region test by running the nested
`anova()` comparison yourself (you did this in 2.3). Report the actual F and
p-value, state whether the AI's numbers match, and write the correct
one-sentence conclusion about region. (2 pts)
